newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador Congress to appoint new interim president.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador Congress to appoint new interim president.

text.p: Ecuador's congressional leader Fabian Alarcon was expected on Tuesday to become interim president for the second time in five days, political sources said, capping a turbulent week in Ecuadorean politics.

Congress was scheduled to hold an extraordinary session at 4 p.m. (2100 GMT) to appoint a leader to rule until August 1998, following the dramatic dismissal last week of populist leader Abdala Bucaram.

Ecuador's shaky transition process, which at one point saw three people claiming the presidency, was still clouded by interim president Rosalia Arteaga's insistence that the Constitution be changed and the possibly she might not step down.
If Congress appoints Alarcon, Ecuador "will enter a period of congressional dictatorship," she told reporters late on Monday. She is the the first woman president in Ecuador's 167-year history.

But amid accusations that she was clinging to power, Arteaga appeared ready to bow to pressure. "There is such an intense pressure that we don't know how the president will be able to resist," one of her close advisers told Reuters.

In a brief interview with reporters on Monday night, Arteaga said: "Congress must first reform the Constitution and then appoint a president. I am not clinging to power here because I know it's a completely transitional situation."
In an apparent response to accusations she was pushed forward by the military, Arteaga said: "There is no puppet at the head of the country."

A 40-year-old lawyer and former education minister, Arteaga became head of a caretaker government on Sunday in an apparent deal between lawmakers and the armed forces to solve the protracted constitutional and political crisis.

The crisis erupted on Thursday when Bucaram, whose eccentricities earned him the nickname "El Loco" (the madman), was ousted by a divided Congress on the grounds of "mental incompetence." The 44-34 vote followed two days of strikes over government austerity measures.

Arteaga insists no one can assume the presidency until a constitutional reform is passed empowering Congress to appoint presidents. Her advisers say without this reform, which must be approved by a two-thirds majority of the 82-member Congress, legislators have no authority to name a president.
Alarcon, 49, said on Monday he could count on the backing of up to 60 congressmen, meaning he would have the necessary votes to pass a constitutional reform.
The accord paving the way for him to be president on Aug. 10, 1998, specified that he could be appointed by a simple majority of Congress, without any constitutional reforms.
Sounding confident that he would be the next interim president, Alarcon said: "The transitional year will lay the foundations to emerge from this terrible situation."
"The relationship between legislators and the executive power will be one of cordiality," he added, in an apparent reference to Bucaram's abrasive style.
He said Ecuador would have to go through a period of economic hardship. "There will be austerity ... but one will have to explain where the money goes," he said.
Alarcon was voted in as president for the first time on Thursday but Bucaram refused to step down until Sunday when the military withdrew its support.
Bucaram called Tuesday's congressional vote as a sham and a "national disgrace."

"Some countries won't see kindly that Ecuador has a president (who is the) product of a dictatorship," he told Reuters at his home in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil. "This is the result of a coup and we all know that."

Bucaram, whose colourful rule lasted only six months, said he would start an international tour next weekend to explain how he was victim of a military-backed "congressional coup." He planned to go to the United States and several Latin American countries, including Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Peru, Colombia and Panama.
He said he would call for a nationwide march on Feb. 26 towards Quito "to reinstate the president elected by the people."
